title: Out of Egypt I Called My Son
summary: God remembers Israel's childhood: he loved the nation, called it out of Egypt, taught it to walk, and fed it, yet the more he called, the farther Israel ran to the Baals. Judgment by Assyria is coming. Then God's own heart recoils from destroying Ephraim completely, and he promises that his children will one day come trembling home when he roars like a lion.
story: After the harvest of judgment in chapter 10, Hosea turns from the image of marriage that dominated his early chapters to the image of a parent and child. The chapter reaches back to the exodus, the founding event of Israel's life, when God rescued a family of slaves from Egypt and made them his people. It is one of the tenderest passages in the Old Testament, and it explains why the story does not end with Samaria's fall. God's judgment is real, but his love is older and deeper, and it will have the last word. The promise of return in verses 10 and 11 anticipates the call to repentance and the healing that close the book in chapter 14.
historical:
The chapter looks back more than it looks around. The exodus from Egypt, traditionally placed in either the fifteenth or the thirteenth century BC depending on how the evidence is weighed, is the moment God called Israel his son (Exodus 4:22-23). The wilderness years and the settlement in Canaan followed, and with them Israel's attraction to the Baals, the storm and fertility gods of the Canaanites.

The threat in the present is Assyria, which under Tiglath-pileser III (reigned 745-727 BC) and his successors was expanding west and reducing Israel to a vassal state. Verse 5 combines two images: Israel will go back to Egypt, a symbol of the slavery it was rescued from, and it will be ruled by Assyria. Some Israelites may well have fled to Egypt, and Israel's last king, Hoshea, sought Egyptian help against Assyria (2 Kings 17:4), but the main fulfillment came with the Assyrian conquest of Samaria in 722 BC and the deportation of much of its population. The chapter's promise that exiles will come trembling from Egypt and Assyria (verse 11) speaks to a people who would soon be scattered in both directions.
cultural:
Hosea draws on the ordinary life of a household. A parent in ancient Israel taught a toddler to walk, carried the child in their arms, and fed them by hand. Verse 4 shifts to the care of work animals: a good farmer led an ox with cords, eased the yoke from its jaw, and bent down to give it food. Both pictures describe a God who cares for his people with patience and physical tenderness. In both pictures God stoops to his people's level.

Admah and Zeboiim (verse 8) were cities of the plain destroyed along with Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 10:19; Deuteronomy 29:23). Hosea's hearers would recognize them as bywords for total destruction. For God to ask how he could make Israel like them is to say that the full sentence Israel deserves is one he cannot bring himself to carry out. The lion's roar in verse 10 was a familiar sound in the thickets of the Jordan valley; here it is not the roar of an attacker but a summons that calls scattered children home.
literary: The chapter is spoken almost entirely in God's own voice, and it moves like a parent's anguished speech. Verses 1 to 4 remember love given; verses 5 to 7 announce the judgment that ingratitude has earned; verses 8 and 9 break off in four questions ("How could I give you up, O Ephraim?") and a reversal of feeling; verses 10 and 11 describe a homecoming. The Hebrew of verse 8 says God's heart has turned over within him, the same verb used for the overthrow of Sodom and its sister cities: the overturning happens inside God rather than to Israel. Verse 12 begins a new section in the Hebrew text (which numbers it 12:1) and serves as a hinge into the accusations of chapter 12.

outline.t: How could I give you up
The lion's roar and the children's return

doctrines.note: Verse 9 grounds God's mercy in his holiness: "For I am God and not man". Human anger often runs to its limit, but God's holiness includes a love that restrains his wrath. The chapter shows that God's justice and compassion are not rivals within him.

Israel's relationship with God began with his initiative in the exodus, before Israel had done anything. The covenant is framed here as sonship: God is the parent who called, taught, and fed his child.

The promise of return in verses 10 and 11 shows that salvation depends finally on God's unwillingness to let his people go. They come home because he roars and calls, not because they found their own way back.

words.note: Ahav, to love. The chapter opens with it: "When Israel was a child, I loved him". It is the ordinary Hebrew word for love, used of parents, spouses, and friends, and in Deuteronomy for God's choosing love for Israel (Deuteronomy 7:8). Here it names affection that came first and explains everything that follows.

Shuv, to turn or return, here in the sense of repent. Verse 5 plays on the word: because Israel refused to return to God, it will return to Egypt. Shuv is Hosea's great word for repentance, and it will open the book's final chapter (14:1).

Nichum, compassion or comfort. In verse 8 God says "My compassion is stirred", using a rare word related to the verb for being moved to pity or changing one's course. It describes a surge of tender feeling that overrides the sentence of destruction.

Qadosh, holy. God calls himself "the Holy One among you". Holiness means God's otherness, his difference from everything created. Surprisingly, it is this holiness that makes him merciful: he is not driven by wounded pride the way a human ruler might be.

christ: Matthew quotes verse 1 when Joseph takes the infant Jesus to Egypt and later brings him back: "Out of Egypt I called My son" (Matthew 2:15). Hosea was speaking of the nation's past, not predicting a future event, and Matthew's use does not depend on reading it as a prediction. He is reading Jesus as the one who sums up Israel's story in his own life: God's true Son who goes down into Egypt, comes out, is tested in the wilderness, and remains faithful where the nation had failed. The chapter's portrait of God also prepares for the gospel. The Father who cannot give up his wayward child is the Father of Jesus's parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15:11-32), and the God whose heart recoils from destroying his people is the God who, in the New Testament's telling, takes judgment on himself in his Son.

hard.q: How can Matthew say a verse about the exodus was fulfilled in Jesus?
hard.a: Read on its own, Hosea 11:1 recalls a past event, the exodus, and it is not framed as a prediction. Some readers have concluded that Matthew misused the verse. The main responses focus on what Matthew means by fulfillment. Many interpreters call his reading typological: the patterns of Israel's history (sonship, exile, rescue) find their fullest expression in Jesus, who is the true Israel and the Son in a unique sense. Others point out that Hosea himself goes on to promise a new exodus from Egypt and Assyria (11:10-11), so the prophet already expected God's past act to be repeated in a greater way. On either view, Matthew is not claiming that Hosea foresaw Jesus's childhood; he is claiming that Jesus's life completes the story Hosea was telling.

questions: Hosea pictures God teaching a child to walk and bending down to feed his people. Which image of God's care speaks most to you, and why?
God asks, "How could I give you up?" What does this chapter suggest about how God feels toward people who have wandered from him?
Verse 9 links God's mercy to his holiness. How does that change the way you think about what holiness means?
